case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant’s supervised-release term continues to run (earning credit toward expiration) during the time she is a fugitive/absconds from supervision, or instead is tolled so that time spent absconding does not count.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (particularly the supervised-release framework and the jurisdictional/extension provision in § 3583(i), as implicated by the fugitive-tolling question).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rico (supported by defense-oriented amici) argues that she is entitled to credit for the supervised-release time that elapsed while she was absconding because Congress did not authorize “fugitive tolling” in the supervised-release statute. In her view, courts may not create an equitable tolling doctrine that effectively extends a term of supervised release beyond its statutory end date; instead, the government must proceed within the statute’s express mechanisms (notably § 3583(i)) and within the supervised-release term as written. She also points to separation-of-powers and jurisdictional concerns—i.e., that extending supervision by judge-made tolling resembles adding punishment beyond what Congress prescribed—and relies on arguments analogizing to strict statutory time limits discussed in Supreme Court precedent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that a supervisee should not be able to benefit from her own wrongdoing by running out the clock while a fugitive. The government’s position is that a term of supervised release is not meaningfully “served” during periods when the defendant absconds and is not under supervision, and therefore the supervised-release clock should not continue to run. Under this view, tolling prevents absconders from avoiding revocation and related consequences for violations (including new drug dealing) simply by disappearing until the nominal end date.
key_precedents: United States v. Watson (Ninth Circuit precedent referenced in the record)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is that fugitive tolling reflects a background principle about what it means to “serve” a supervised-release term, so it is interpretation rather than atextual extension. But in this statutory scheme Congress spoke directly to when supervised release “does not run” in § 3624(e) and separately cabined post-expiration revocation authority in § 3583(i) to cases with a timely warrant or summons; as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan emphasize, adding an implied fugitive-tolling rule would blunt that calibrated trigger and effectively expand the court’s power beyond Congress’s expressed conditions. Justice Alito’s policy concern that absconders should not profit from wrongdoing is serious, yet under a minimalist, precedent-respecting approach (and consistent with Bowles’s caution against equitable enlargement of congressionally set limits), the remedy is for the government to use § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons mechanism or for Congress to amend the statute. I would therefore keep the holding narrow: absent an express statutory basis (including § 3583(i)’s trigger), supervised-release time runs as written even if the defendant absconds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest contention—that a supervised-release “term” must mean time actually supervised and that a fugitive should not profit from wrongdoing—cannot supply a tolling rule Congress did not enact. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Congress expressly provided a clock-stopping rule in § 3624(e) (“does not run”) and then separately set a jurisdiction-preserving, warrant-or-summons precondition for post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i); that structure strongly negates any additional, judge-made “fugitive tolling.” Treating § 3583(i)’s time-and-process limits as implicitly extendable by equity would conflict with Bowles v. Russell’s admonition that courts may not enlarge congressionally fixed jurisdictional time limits, and would effectively expand punishment exposure beyond the term authorized. The proper remedy for absconders is the statutory one—timely issuance of a warrant or summons—not an atextual doctrine that rewrites Congress’s detailed scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch make the best textual-structure point: § 3624(e) and § 3583(i) are explicit timing provisions, and Bowles counsels caution about judicially enlarging statutory limits. But I do not read § 3583(i) as an exclusive clock-control mechanism; it is a post-expiration jurisdictional backstop keyed to timely process, whereas fugitive tolling goes to the antecedent statutory meaning of whether a defendant is "serv[ing]" the supervised-release term at all while he has made supervision impossible. Justice Kagan’s negative-implication argument is powerful, yet it fails for me because § 3624(e)’s imprisonment tolling solves a different coordination problem and does not purport to define what counts as time “served” under supervision, and Congress reasonably legislated against the settled principle that one cannot profit from flight. Because this interpretation construes the operative concept of service rather than creating a free-floating equitable exception, I do not think Bowles or Johnson/Mont foreclose it, and the practical consequences Roberts acknowledges (absconders running out the clock) confirm Congress likely did not intend that result by silence.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that fugitive tolling reflects a “background principle” about not benefiting from flight and a commonsense understanding that a supervision “term” implies actual supervision. But as Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, Congress made specific, textually grounded timing choices in § 3624(e) (express “does not run” tolling) and § 3583(i) (a warrant-or-summons condition for post-expiration revocation power), and adding an implied absconder tolling rule would function as an atextual expansion of both punishment exposure and judicial authority. Justice Alito’s fairness intuition cannot overcome the structural negative implication and the Bowles-style separation-of-powers concern flagged by Justice Gorsuch: courts should not enlarge congressionally cabined timing/jurisdiction rules through equity when Congress supplied a concrete safeguard (timely process under § 3583(i)). The government’s enforcement concern is real, but it is addressed by issuing a warrant promptly, not by converting contested “absconding” findings into clock-stopping that will fall hardest on defendants with the least stability and access to counsel.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that a supervised-release “term” presupposes actual supervision and that background anti-profiting-from-flight principles mean absconding time is not “served”—has force as a policy matter, but it does not fit this statute’s enacted architecture. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Congress expressly identified when supervised release “does not run” in § 3624(e) and then carefully limited post-expiration revocation power in § 3583(i) to cases with a timely warrant or summons; implying fugitive tolling would effectively add a new clock-stopping rule that expands both the term and the court’s post-expiration authority beyond those text-anchored conditions. Bowles’s caution against judicial enlargement of congressionally cabined timing/jurisdiction rules makes me especially reluctant to treat “background principles” as a substitute for the negative implication from Congress’s specific tolling choices. The workable, coherent solution within the statute is the government’s use of § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons mechanism, not a judge-made overlay that risks inconsistent absconding determinations and bypasses Congress’s procedural trigger.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s background-principles argument—that a fugitive cannot "serve" supervised release and therefore time must be suspended—has force as a policy intuition, but it asks us to supply a tolling rule Congress did not enact in a statute that already specifies when time "does not run" (§ 3624(e)) and when revocation authority survives expiration (§ 3583(i)). Justice Alito’s distinction between § 3583(i) as a mere post-expiration "backstop" and fugitive tolling as a definition of "serving" the term still collapses into the same problem: it would enlarge the court’s post-expiration "power … to revoke" without satisfying § 3583(i)’s warrant-or-summons condition, effectively rewriting an express limitation. Bowles reinforces the separation-of-powers concern here: where Congress has set the conditions for extending jurisdiction and punishment exposure, we may not create an equitable add-on—especially when Congress supplied a concrete remedy (timely warrant/summons) for absconders. I therefore remain with the petitioner; any perceived enforcement gap is for Congress to close, not for us to paper over by implication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the strongest textual-structure point: § 3624(e) and § 3583(i) are detailed timing provisions, and negative implication plus Bowles counsels caution about judge-made extensions. But I do not think recognizing fugitive tolling "extends" the term so much as it interprets what it means to "serve" a supervised-release term—time when the defendant has made supervision impossible is not plausibly time served toward completion, a background understanding Congress can be assumed to have legislated against. Section 3583(i) answers a different question (post-expiration adjudicatory power when process was timely issued) and need not be treated as the exclusive mechanism for situations where the term itself never effectively ran because of flight. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern is serious, but on my methodology the best reading reconciles text with longstanding anti-profiting-from-wrongdoing principles and the practical function of supervised release rather than creating an atextual equitable exception.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito make the best opposing point that a supervised-release “term” conceptually presupposes actual supervision and that a fugitive should not profit from wrongdoing, but that intuition cannot supply an unstated tolling rule in a detailed statutory scheme. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress expressly specified when supervised release “does not run” in § 3624(e) and separately provided a calibrated, warrant-or-summons-triggered mechanism in § 3583(i) for post-expiration revocation power; reading in fugitive tolling would effectively rewrite those provisions and dilute § 3583(i)’s precondition. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern and Bowles’s warning against equitable enlargement of congressionally cabined timing/jurisdiction rules reinforce that we should not extend punishment or court power beyond the lines Congress drew. The government’s policy problem is real, but the statutory answer is to use § 3583(i)’s timely process device, not to add atextual tolling by judicial doctrine.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh make the best practical and “background principle” case: it feels wrong to let an absconder run out the clock, and one can say he is not really being supervised. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress already wrote two precise timing mechanisms—§ 3624(e) (when the term “does not run”) and § 3583(i) (post-expiration revocation only if a warrant/summons issues before expiration)—and a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would effectively bypass § 3583(i)’s procedural safeguard and enlarge exposure to punishment and court power beyond those lines. Bowles’s warning against equitable enlargement of congressionally cabined time/jurisdiction limits strengthens, rather than weakens, my separation-of-powers concern here: even if tolling is recast as “what it means to serve” the term, the legal effect is still to extend the term and the court’s authority absent the statutory trigger. The government’s unfairness argument is real, but under a progressive pragmatist lens that values procedural regularity, the answer is to require timely process under § 3583(i) (or legislative change), not to create a contested, fact-intensive absconding tolling doctrine with uneven and potentially inequitable application.

John Roberts.reasoning: The supervised-release statutes already specify when the clock stops: 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) expressly tolls supervised release during imprisonment, and Congress separately provided a targeted, jurisdiction-preserving mechanism in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(i) to revoke after expiration only when a warrant or summons issued before the term ends. Reading an additional, judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule into § 3583 would risk extending supervision beyond the term Congress authorized and would circumvent § 3583(i)’s carefully drawn limits, raising institutional and separation-of-powers concerns. Under Bowles v. Russell, this Court has been reluctant to create equitable exceptions that effectively enlarge congressionally prescribed time limits, and the negative implication from § 3624(e)’s express tolling provision counsels against implying another. A narrow, text-anchored holding rejecting fugitive tolling best preserves statutory boundaries while leaving enforcement to Congress’s chosen tools (including prompt issuance of a warrant/summons under § 3583(i)).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The supervised-release statute does not authorize a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule, and under a strict textualist reading courts may not add such an extension mechanism. Congress provided an express, jurisdictional provision for delayed revocation in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(i), allowing revocation after expiration only when a warrant or summons issued before expiration; the express specification of that limited extension implies exclusion of other implied extensions (expressio unius). Treating § 3583(i)’s jurisdictional limits as subject to equitable tolling would contradict this Court’s insistence on strict adherence to congressionally set jurisdictional time limits, see Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007). Whatever policy concerns exist about absconders “running out the clock” are for Congress to address, not the courts, given separation-of-powers limits on expanding punishment beyond the statutory term.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A supervised-release “term” under 18 U.S.C. § 3583 contemplates actual supervision; when a defendant absconds, she is not being supervised at all, and it would be perverse to treat that period as time “served” toward expiration. Section 3583(i) reflects Congress’s concern that courts retain authority to address violations when timely action is initiated, and reading the statute to allow fugitives to run out the clock would undermine that framework and invite strategic evasion of revocation. Although 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) contains an express no-running rule for imprisonment, that provision addresses a distinct situation and does not compel the conclusion that Congress affirmatively required credit for fugitive time; practical consequences and the longstanding principle that one may not benefit from one’s own wrongdoing support tolling here. This approach avoids an interpretation that would seriously impair law enforcement’s ability to enforce supervised release and protect the public from ongoing criminal conduct during absconding.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The supervised-release statutes provide a specific tolling rule in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (imprisonment for a new conviction) and a distinct, limited mechanism for post-expiration enforcement in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(i) (warrant/summons issued before expiration). Under United States v. Johnson, 529 U.S. 53 (2000), when Congress enumerates particular exceptions to when supervised-release time “does not run,” courts should not create additional judge-made exceptions, especially where doing so effectively lengthens punishment beyond the term Congress authorized. Allowing fugitive tolling would also circumvent the limits Congress placed in § 3583(i) and raise separation-of-powers concerns by permitting courts to extend supervision through equitable doctrine rather than statutory text. The government’s fairness argument is substantial, but Congress accounted for absconding-related enforcement through warrants and retained jurisdiction under § 3583(i), and that is where the remedy must come from.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3583 creates a detailed supervised-release scheme, and when Congress wanted tolling it said so expressly (as in § 3624(e), interpreted in Mont v. United States), while separately limiting the court’s post-expiration revocation power to the specific conditions in § 3583(i). Reading an atextual “fugitive tolling” doctrine into § 3583 would risk doing exactly what Bowles v. Russell cautions against—creating equitable exceptions that extend congressionally cabined court power, especially where § 3583(i) speaks in jurisdictional terms (“[t]he power of the court to revoke”). The government’s policy concern is real, but the statute supplies a workable mechanism: timely issuance of a warrant or summons under § 3583(i), rather than judge-made clock-stopping that effectively lengthens the term beyond its stated end. Given supervised release’s statutory novelty and Congress’s choice to address tolling expressly in related provisions, the better textual and structural reading is that time continues to run absent § 3583(i)’s trigger.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3583 sets out a detailed supervised-release scheme, and Congress specifically addressed post-expiration authority in § 3583(i) by extending the court’s power to revoke only when a warrant or summons issues before the term expires—an express limitation that strongly counsels against implying an additional, judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule. Under the negative-implication canon, where Congress “includes particular language in one section . . . but omits it in another,” we generally presume the omission is intentional, City & County of San Francisco v. EPA, 145 S. Ct. 704, 713–14 (2025), and § 3583(i) reads like Congress’s chosen fix for absconders rather than an invitation for courts to extend supervision beyond the statutory end date. Treating the term as tolled would effectively enlarge punishment and judicial jurisdiction without textual authorization, raising separation-of-powers concerns and echoing this Court’s insistence on strict adherence to statutory time limits in Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007). Whatever the policy appeal, it is for Congress—not courts—to add tolling; where liberty is at stake and the statute is at least ambiguous, the rule of lenity also points against extending supervised release by implication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A supervised-release term is designed to be served under supervision, and traditional principles long recognized that a defendant should not profit by evading the court’s authority; time spent as a fugitive is not meaningfully “served,” so tolling fits the history-and-tradition backdrop against which Congress legislated. Section 3624(e)’s express tolling rule for imprisonment does not, by negative implication, foreclose fugitive tolling because it addresses a distinct situation (concurrent imprisonment) and was needed to calibrate when imprisonment pauses supervision, while abscondment implicates the settled rule that flight suspends the running of time. Section 3583(i) is best read as a narrow, practical backstop for late-issued warrants/summonses and delayed adjudication, not as the exclusive mechanism that forces courts to credit fugitives with time they refused to be supervised. This construction avoids an unworkable regime where absconders can “run out the clock,” and it respects judicial restraint by applying established background principles rather than creating an expansive new punishment beyond § 3583’s framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The supervised-release statutes specify when a term "does not run"—most notably in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) for imprisonment—yet § 3583 contains no comparable text authorizing tolling for absconding, and § 3583(i) supplies only a limited, jurisdiction-preserving mechanism keyed to a warrant or summons issued before expiration. Reading an atextual “fugitive tolling” doctrine into § 3583 would effectively extend the term beyond its statutory end date and risks altering a jurisdictional rule by equity, which this Court has cautioned against in cases like Bowles v. Russell. Mont v. United States illustrates that tolling turns on statutory text and structure, not a free-floating policy judgment that a defendant should not “benefit” from wrongdoing. Given Congress’s express choice to address delayed revocation through § 3583(i), courts should not add an additional, judge-made tolling rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3583 sets a term of supervised release as part of the sentence, and Congress supplied a specific, tightly drawn mechanism for late revocation when the term has otherwise expired—§ 3583(i)—without authorizing a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule that effectively extends the term beyond its statutory end date. In light of Bowles v. Russell’s insistence that courts may not create equitable exceptions to statutory time limits that define jurisdiction, I am reluctant to treat supervised-release expiration as judicially malleable where Congress has spoken to timing and post-expiration authority. United States v. Johnson (2000) and Mont v. United States (2019) show that this Court will follow statutory text to determine when supervised-release time counts and has required clear authorization for crediting or altering supervision, which counsels against importing an atextual tolling doctrine here. Procedural fairness and separation-of-powers concerns are heightened when tolling turns on contested allegations of absconding and risks extending supervision (and exposure to imprisonment upon revocation) beyond what Congress prescribed.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether time on supervised release counts toward completion of the supervised-release term when the supervisee absconds and is not reporting to or being monitored by probation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (particularly the operation of supervised release and the court’s authority to revoke or extend supervision; the dispute centers on whether any form of “fugitive tolling” applies notwithstanding the statute’s text, including § 3583(i)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rico argues that supervised release continues to run according to the statute’s fixed term even if a person absconds, because Congress provided specific tolling/extension mechanisms in § 3583 (not a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule). She contends that allowing tolling for absconding is an atextual expansion of judicial power, conflicts with jurisdictional/time-limit principles reflected in cases like Bowles v. Russell, and creates unfairness by transforming a determinate supervision term into an indeterminate one without clear statutory authorization.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that a supervisee should not receive “credit” for supervised release while intentionally evading supervision, because supervised release is a monitoring/rehabilitation period that cannot function when the person is a fugitive. The government contends that fugitive tolling is consistent with § 3583’s purpose and structure, prevents absconders from benefiting from their misconduct, and preserves the court’s ability to impose consequences for violations (including drug-dealing or drug-possession violations) that occur during supervision but are not addressed until the defendant is located.
key_precedents: United States v. Watson (Ninth Circuit precedent referenced in the district-court excerpt; cited as binding on the district court)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s structural point—that Congress expressly tolls in § 3624(e) and separately provided a narrow post-expiration mechanism in § 3583(i)—is the most serious obstacle, and it narrows the room for any implied rule. But I remain persuaded that this case can be decided as a question of what it means to “serve” a term of supervised release: deliberate absconding that makes supervision impossible is not “service,” so the statutory “term” has not run, and § 3583(i) operates as a jurisdictional backstop when the term has otherwise been running but adjudication is delayed. Justice Thomas’s Bowles-based concern has force if we are equitably extending a deadline, yet on my approach we are not extending jurisdiction past an expired term; we are determining the term never completed because the defendant was not under supervision in any meaningful sense. To protect administrability and fairness, I would adopt Justice Kavanaugh’s limiting principle: tolling only upon clear findings of intentional flight/absconding, avoiding the indeterminacy Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett warn about.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest functional point: an absconder is not really “serving” supervision, so tolling is merely definitional rather than equitable. But that reframing still lacks textual footing—§ 3583 sets a determinate “term,” and Congress provided a specific, triggered extension in § 3583(i) (pre-expiration warrant or summons) while using explicit tolling language elsewhere, as Justice Kagan notes with § 3624(e); under a textualist method, those choices foreclose an implied fugitive-tolling doctrine. Roberts’s characterization of § 3583(i) as a mere “backstop” cannot justify reading it as nonexclusive and thereby converting a fixed statutory endpoint into an indeterminate one based on policy concerns. Johnson and Mont, invoked by Kavanaugh and Alito, describe supervised release’s function and apply enacted tolling mechanisms, but they do not authorize courts to add a new tolling rule Congress conspicuously omitted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s text-and-structure argument (express tolling in § 3624(e) plus the warrant/summons condition in § 3583(i)) is the most serious objection, but it still presumes that a supervised-release “term” necessarily runs as a calendar regardless of whether supervision is actually being carried out. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh that § 3583(i) is best read as a limited delayed-adjudication/jurisdictional backstop—addressing late revocation proceedings when the Government acts in time—not as a comprehensive definition of what it means to “serve” supervised release during deliberate flight. Justice Thomas’s Bowles-based concern has force only if fugitive tolling is an equitable extension of a jurisdictional deadline; on my view, it is instead a textual interpretation of “supervised release” as operative supervision, so an absconder is not “serving” the term while making supervision impossible. Cabining the rule to intentional absconding with clear findings answers Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Barrett’s indeterminacy worries without adopting a construction that rewards evasion and frustrates Congress’s public-safety design.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that fugitive tolling is merely interpreting what it means to “serve” supervised release—has intuitive appeal, but it still functionally extends a congressionally fixed term without a textual trigger. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett stress, Congress enacted explicit tolling in § 3624(e) and a tightly conditioned post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i) (requiring a warrant or summons before expiration); treating § 3583(i) as just a “backstop,” as Chief Justice Roberts proposes, drains that condition of meaningful force and authorizes an additional judge-made extension. Johnson and Mont, invoked by Justice Kavanaugh, do not supply the missing authorization here because they interpret enacted rules about when time counts, whereas this case asks us to create a new category of non-counting time that Congress conspicuously omitted. Given the real-world risk that “absconding” labels will fall hardest on unstable and vulnerable people, I cannot accept an indeterminate supervision regime by implication when the statute already provides the government a clear, timely tool in § 3583(i).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point: that tolling is not “equitable” but flows from the meaning of “serve” a “term” of supervised release when a defendant intentionally absconds. But that definitional move still collides with Congress’s timing architecture—§ 3624(e) expressly tolls for imprisonment and § 3583(i) supplies a narrow post-expiration revocation backstop conditioned on a pre-expiration warrant or summons—so reading an additional, uncodified absconding-tolling rule effectively makes the term indeterminate and sidelines § 3583(i)’s trigger. Justice Alito’s reliance on Johnson’s functional account helps explain why supervision matters, yet Johnson and Mont both operate within express statutory mechanisms; they do not license us to extend restraint beyond the statutory endpoint by recharacterizing tolling as “service.” I remain persuaded by Justice Thomas’s separation-of-powers concern: even cabined to “intentional absconding,” the proposed rule adds a new suspension doctrine Congress conspicuously did not enact, and the administrability fix cannot supply the missing text.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh offer the strongest counter: that an absconder is not “serving” supervised release and so the clock should not run, making tolling a matter of definition rather than equity. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett explain, Congress already supplied the timing architecture—express tolling in § 3624(e) and a narrow, expressly conditioned post-expiration revocation authority in § 3583(i) triggered only by a pre-expiration warrant or summons—which is powerful evidence that courts may not add an unwritten absconding suspension that effectively makes § 3583(i)’s trigger nonexclusive. Johnson’s functional discussion of supervised release’s purposes and Mont’s recognition of tolling where Congress provided it do not authorize converting a determinate “term” into an indeterminate restraint by implication; doing so raises the separation-of-powers concerns Justice Thomas flags (Bowles-style) and, at minimum, triggers lenity where Congress chose precision. The Government’s policy worry is real, but the statute’s answer is to use § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons mechanism (and other enacted sanctions), not a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine recast as “service.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett press the strongest structural point: Congress expressly provided tolling in § 3624(e) and a warrant/summons-based post-expiration mechanism in § 3583(i), suggesting no further tolling by implication. But that inference depends on the premise that the supervised-release “term” necessarily runs as a clock even when the defendant’s deliberate flight makes the congressionally required supervision impossible; I continue to read “serve a term of supervised release” as connoting actual, operative subjection to supervision, consistent with Johnson’s functional account and Mont’s recognition that supervised release is part of the sentence’s administration. In that light, § 3583(i) works as Chief Justice Roberts describes—a jurisdictional backstop for adjudicating violations when the term is otherwise being served—and it does not clearly answer the antecedent question whether an intentional absconder is serving the term at all. Justice Thomas’s Bowles warning is important, but I see this as statutory interpretation of “serve” in context, not an equitable extension of a jurisdictional deadline; cabining the rule to intentional absconding with clear findings addresses Justice Sotomayor’s administrability and fairness concerns without creating an open-ended, judge-made extension in ordinary noncompliance cases.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point—that fugitive tolling can be framed as a textual interpretation of whether an absconder is “serving” a “term” of supervised release—has intuitive and linguistic pull, but it still cannot be squared with Congress’s explicit timing architecture. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Congress provided express tolling in § 3624(e) and a carefully conditioned post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i) requiring a pre-expiration warrant or summons; treating absconding as an implicit suspension would effectively bypass § 3583(i)’s prerequisite and convert a determinate term into an indeterminate one. Johnson and Mont (invoked by Justice Kavanaugh) do not supply authority to add a new tolling trigger; they interpret enacted triggers and the function of supervised release within sentencing, underscoring that when tolling is authorized, Congress says so. Policy concerns about “running out the clock” are serious, but under a textualist approach they are addressed through § 3583(i) and other enacted sanctions, not a judge-made supplementation of the statutory endpoint.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point—that an absconder is not really “serving” supervision and fugitive tolling can be framed as interpretation of “term” rather than an equitable add-on—but that move still alters the statutory endpoint Congress specified. As Justice Kagan notes, Congress paired an express tolling rule in § 3624(e) with a carefully cabined post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i) (triggered by a pre-expiration warrant or summons), and reading an additional, implied suspension for absconding effectively bypasses that condition and converts a determinate term into an indeterminate one. Johnson and Mont do not supply authority to extend restraint absent a statutory trigger; they interpret enacted mechanisms and purposes, not a judicially supplied “service” exception. Even with Justice Roberts’s proposed limitation to intentional absconding, the procedural-fairness costs and separation-of-powers concern remain because the scope and duration of restraint would hinge on contested post hoc findings rather than Congress’s chosen timing rules.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3583 establishes supervised release as a court-imposed period of supervision with enforceable conditions, and it strains the statutory scheme to treat a defendant as “serving” that term while intentionally evading all supervision. Reading § 3583(i) as the exclusive timing mechanism for post-expiration action would allow an absconder to run out the clock and defeat the judgment’s supervisory component, undermining the statute’s evident function and institutional legitimacy of supervised-release sentences. This conclusion fits the Court’s approach in Johnson v. United States, 529 U.S. 694 (2000), which treated supervised release as a distinct, operative part of the sentence and construed § 3583 to preserve meaningful judicial authority to enforce it. A narrow holding limited to deliberate absconding avoids indeterminate extensions in ordinary cases and respects federalism by applying a uniform federal rule to a federal sentencing regime.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 establishes a determinate term of supervised release and specifies the limited circumstance in which a court may act after that term expires: § 3583(i) permits delayed revocation only if a warrant or summons issued before expiration. Recognizing a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule would add an atextual exception that effectively extends the court’s power beyond the statute’s expressed limits, converting a fixed term into an indeterminate one without congressional authorization. Our jurisdictional/time-limit cases caution against judicially created equitable extensions where Congress has spoken in jurisdictional terms, see Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), and § 3583(i) reflects Congress’s chosen mechanism for preserving authority when violations are discovered late. Whatever policy appeal the Government’s argument has, it must be implemented by Congress through text, not by courts through common-law supplementation of § 3583.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Supervised release under 18 U.S.C. § 3583 is a period of actual supervision; a defendant who absconds is not being supervised at all, so crediting that time would convert the statutory scheme into a reward for evasion and seriously undermine supervision’s rehabilitative and public-safety functions. Nothing in § 3583’s text affirmatively entitles a fugitive to have the term continue running while she deliberately prevents the Government from carrying out court-ordered monitoring, and the statute should not be read to produce that perverse practical consequence. Section 3583(i)’s post-expiration revocation jurisdiction (conditioned on issuance of a warrant or summons before expiration) is best understood as a backstop for ordinary cases, not as a guarantee that absconders can run out the clock by avoiding supervision until the fixed end date. Bowles v. Russell’s insistence on respecting statutory limits does not require reading § 3583 to mandate a loophole that defeats enforcement; here the more faithful reading treats absconding as suspending the running of a supervision period that cannot operate in the defendant’s self-created absence.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3583(i) is the provision Congress enacted to address delayed revocation—authorizing post-expiration revocation only when a warrant or summons issued before expiration—so a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule that pauses the term rewrites the statutory scheme and expands judicial power beyond the text. Under Bowles v. Russell, courts may not create equitable exceptions that effectively extend congressionally fixed time limits where Congress has spoken to the court’s power, and § 3583(i) expressly cabins that power. Practical fairness also cuts against tolling: it risks turning a determinate supervision term into an indeterminate one, disproportionately harming supervisees with unstable housing or mental illness who may “abscond” in ways short of intentional evasion. If Congress wishes to add tolling for absconding, it can do so explicitly; courts should enforce the statute as written and rely on § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons mechanism for timely enforcement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3583 sets a determinate term of supervised release and supplies specific mechanisms for dealing with violations discovered late, most notably § 3583(i), which extends revocation jurisdiction only if a warrant or summons issues before expiration; that carefully delimited scheme leaves little room for a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule that effectively lengthens the term itself. Congress also demonstrated elsewhere that it knows how to write tolling rules when it wants them (e.g., § 3624(e)’s custody tolling), and its choice in § 3583(i) to extend jurisdiction rather than toll time should be respected as a matter of statutory coherence. Allowing tolling would create indeterminate supervision and potentially extend supervision beyond statutory maxima, an atextual expansion of judicial power inconsistent with the Court’s insistence in Bowles v. Russell that courts may not create equitable exceptions to congressionally prescribed time limits. Workability concerns are addressed by § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons mechanism and by separate prosecution for new crimes, without rewriting the statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3583 sets out a determinate term of supervised release and specifies the limited circumstance in which a court may act after that term ends: under § 3583(i), only when a warrant or summons issues before expiration may the court revoke “for any period reasonably necessary” to adjudicate the violation. Recognizing a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule would effectively create an additional, atextual mechanism for extending supervision and the court’s power beyond the statute’s carefully drawn limits, raising separation-of-powers concerns and undermining clear jurisdictional/time rules. Bowles v. Russell cautions against judicially crafted exceptions to congressionally prescribed timing limits, and the same principle applies where Congress has provided an express delayed-revocation provision rather than an open-ended tolling regime. To the extent ambiguity remains in a criminal supervision statute affecting the length of restraint, the rule of lenity counsels against enlarging the term by implied tolling.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3583’s structure and purpose contemplate a real, workable period of “postconfinement monitoring,” and a supervisee who absconds is not being supervised in any meaningful sense; counting that time would undermine the sentencing court’s lawful judgment and create perverse incentives. Consistent with Mont v. United States, 587 U.S. 514 (2019), and the Court’s reasoning in Johnson v. United States, 529 U.S. 53 (2000), supervised release is not simply a clock that runs regardless of whether the defendant is actually subject to supervision’s burdens and benefits. Petitioner’s reliance on § 3583(i) and Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), is not persuasive because recognizing fugitive tolling does not expand jurisdiction beyond Congress’s limits so much as interpret when the supervised-release “term” is actually being served for purposes of § 3583’s operation. As a practical matter and as a matter of tradition (e.g., the escape rule that time at large does not count toward service), the better reading is that absconding pauses the supervised-release term until the defendant is again available for supervision.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of the supervised-release scheme does not authorize a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule: Congress expressly provided tolling in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (imprisonment) and a limited, time-bounded mechanism for delayed revocation jurisdiction in § 3583(i), and that specificity counsels against implying an additional, extra-textual tolling doctrine. Reading fugitive tolling into § 3583 would effectively convert a determinate supervision term into an indeterminate one and expand judicial authority beyond the statute’s limits, despite Congress’s evident attention to timing and jurisdiction in § 3583(i). While the government’s policy concern has force, it cannot overcome the statute’s enacted limits, particularly where time limits and jurisdictional constraints are treated as mandatory and not judicially alterable. Bowles v. Russell reinforces the need for strict adherence to congressionally prescribed temporal/jurisdictional boundaries rather than equitable or common-law supplementation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3583 sets a determinate supervised-release term and specifies the limited circumstance in which a court may act after expiration—§ 3583(i), which requires a warrant or summons issued before the term ends—so importing a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule risks expanding judicial power beyond the statutory text and creating an indeterminate supervision period. That structural choice matters for procedural fairness: Congress provided a clear mechanism to preserve revocation authority when a supervisee cannot be promptly brought before the court, and courts should not circumvent those limits by deeming the term stopped without statutory authorization. While Johnson v. United States recognizes supervised release as “postconfinement monitoring” and “assistance,” it does not hold that absconding automatically tolls the term; instead, it underscores that Congress spoke to timing and post-expiration jurisdiction in the statute. Consistent with Bowles v. Russell’s insistence on respecting congressionally set time limits, I would hold that time continues to run unless the government invokes the tools Congress supplied (including § 3583(i)).
